nutrients.name: Protein
nutrients.role: Builds and repairs muscle, skin, enzymes and antibodies.
nutrients.short: Muscle loss, slow healing and getting sick more often.

nutrients.name: Carbohydrates
nutrients.role: The body's main fuel, and the brain's preferred one.
nutrients.short: Low energy, poor focus and tiring quickly during exercise.

nutrients.name: Fiber
nutrients.role: Keeps digestion regular and feeds healthy gut bacteria.
nutrients.short: Constipation, and blood sugar that swings more after meals.

nutrients.name: Omega-3 fats
nutrients.role: Part of every cell wall; supports heart, brain and eyes.
nutrients.short: Dry skin; low intake over years is linked to heart problems.
nutrients.note: There is no FDA Daily Value for omega-3. This table uses 1.6 g a day, the NIH adequate intake of ALA for men, as the reference. Plants give ALA, which the body converts to EPA and DHA only in small amounts; oily fish gives EPA and DHA directly. USDA does not report omega-3 in this dataset, so only foods listed by NIH have a value.

nutrients.name: Vitamin A
nutrients.role: Lets your eyes see in dim light and keeps skin and immunity healthy.
nutrients.short: Night blindness and more infections.
nutrients.note: Orange and dark-green vegetables give beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.

nutrients.name: Vitamin D
nutrients.role: Helps you absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth.
nutrients.short: Weak, aching bones; rickets in children.
nutrients.note: Few foods contain much vitamin D. Most people get it from sunlight on skin, fortified foods such as milk, or supplements.

nutrients.name: Vitamin E
nutrients.role: An antioxidant that protects cells from damage.
nutrients.short: Rare; can cause nerve and muscle problems.

nutrients.name: Vitamin K
nutrients.role: Makes blood clot when you're cut and helps build bone.
nutrients.short: Bruising easily and bleeding that is slow to stop.
nutrients.note: People on blood thinners such as warfarin should keep vitamin K intake steady; ask your doctor.

nutrients.name: Thiamin
nutrients.role: Turns carbohydrates into energy for nerves and muscles.
nutrients.short: Fatigue, irritability and, when severe, beriberi.

nutrients.name: Riboflavin
nutrients.role: Helps release energy from food and keeps skin and eyes healthy.
nutrients.short: Cracked lips and corners of the mouth, sore throat.

nutrients.name: Niacin
nutrients.role: Needed by hundreds of enzymes that make energy.
nutrients.short: Skin rash in sunlight, digestive trouble; pellagra when severe.
nutrients.note: Values are preformed niacin. The body also makes some niacin from the protein building block tryptophan, so protein-rich foods give more than shown.

nutrients.name: Pantothenic acid
nutrients.role: Helps make energy, hormones and cholesterol.
nutrients.short: Very rare because it is in almost every food.

nutrients.name: Vitamin B6
nutrients.role: Helps build brain chemicals and red blood cells.
nutrients.short: Anemia, skin rash, confusion and low mood.

nutrients.name: Biotin
nutrients.role: Helps break down fats, carbs and protein.
nutrients.short: Rare; thinning hair and a scaly rash.
nutrients.note: USDA does not measure biotin. Values come from the NIH biotin fact sheet, which lists only a few foods, so many foods here simply have no biotin figure.

nutrients.name: Folate
nutrients.role: Needed to make new cells, including red blood cells and DNA.
nutrients.short: Anemia and tiredness. In pregnancy, raises the risk of birth defects.
nutrients.note: Anyone who could become pregnant is usually advised to take a folic acid supplement too.

nutrients.name: Vitamin B12
nutrients.role: Keeps nerves healthy and helps make red blood cells.
nutrients.short: Anemia, tingling hands and feet, memory problems.
nutrients.note: Only animal foods contain reliable B12. Vegans need fortified foods or a supplement.

nutrients.name: Vitamin C
nutrients.role: Builds collagen for skin and gums, and helps absorb iron from plants.
nutrients.short: Bleeding gums and slow wound healing; scurvy when severe.
nutrients.note: Heat destroys some vitamin C, so raw fruit and vegetables keep the most.

nutrients.name: Choline
nutrients.role: A vitamin-like nutrient for memory, muscles and the liver.
nutrients.short: Fatty liver and muscle damage.

nutrients.name: Calcium
nutrients.role: Builds bones and teeth and lets muscles contract.
nutrients.short: Weaker bones over time (osteoporosis).
nutrients.note: Calcium from spinach is poorly absorbed; kale, tofu and dairy are better sources.

nutrients.name: Phosphorus
nutrients.role: Works with calcium in bones and helps store energy.
nutrients.short: Rare; weakness and bone pain.

nutrients.name: Magnesium
nutrients.role: Used by over 300 enzymes; relaxes muscles and steadies heart rhythm.
nutrients.short: Muscle cramps, tiredness and an irregular heartbeat.

nutrients.name: Potassium
nutrients.role: Balances fluids and keeps nerves, muscles and heart working.
nutrients.short: Muscle weakness and cramps; higher blood pressure.

nutrients.name: Iron
nutrients.role: Carries oxygen around the body in red blood cells.
nutrients.short: Iron-deficiency anemia: tiredness, pale skin, feeling cold.
nutrients.note: Iron from plants is absorbed less well. Eating it with vitamin C helps.

nutrients.name: Zinc
nutrients.role: Supports immunity, wound healing, taste and smell.
nutrients.short: Frequent infections, slow healing, loss of taste.

nutrients.name: Copper
nutrients.role: Helps use iron and keeps nerves and blood vessels healthy.
nutrients.short: Rare; anemia and nerve problems.

nutrients.name: Manganese
nutrients.role: Helps form bone and process carbohydrates.
nutrients.short: Very rare.

nutrients.name: Selenium
nutrients.role: Protects cells and helps the thyroid work.
nutrients.short: Rare; weak muscles and thyroid trouble.
nutrients.note: One or two Brazil nuts cover a day. More than a few a day can be too much.

nutrients.name: Iodine
nutrients.role: Needed to make thyroid hormones, which set your metabolism.
nutrients.short: Goiter (swollen thyroid), tiredness, weight gain.
nutrients.note: Iodized salt is the main source for many people. USDA does not report iodine in this dataset, so values come from the USDA/FDA/NIH iodine database as listed by NIH. Seaweed can contain far more than you need.
